etymology: The Christian-ethical tradition governing the moral conditions under which war may be justly waged. Roots in Augustine (City of God, Contra Faustum); systematized by Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II q. 40); refined through the Reformed-confessional and broader Christian tradition. Two principal divisions: jus ad bellum (justice in going to war) and jus in bello (justice in the conduct of war).
biblical_def: The Christian-ethical tradition governing the moral conditions under which war may be justly waged and justly conducted. The tradition has roots in Augustine, was systematized by Thomas Aquinas, and was refined through the Reformed-confessional and broader Christian tradition. The criteria divide into two parts. Jus ad bellum (justice in going to war): (1) just cause (defense against aggression, protection of the innocent, righting of grave wrong); (2) legitimate authority (the lawful magistrate, who alone bears the sword, Romans 13:4 — not private individuals or factions); (3) right intention (the restoration of justice and peace, not conquest, plunder, or revenge); (4) reasonable hope of success; (5) proportionality (the good achieved must outweigh the harm); (6) last resort (war undertaken only after lawful alternatives are exhausted). Jus in bello (justice in the conduct of war): (1) discrimination (combatants may be targeted; non-combatants may not be deliberately targeted); (2) proportionality (the force used must be proportionate to the legitimate military objective). The biblical foundation includes the magistrate's God-given sword-bearing authority (Romans 13:1-4), the OT laws of warfare (Deuteronomy 20), and the broader biblical distinction between lawful civil-magisterial use of the sword and unlawful private vengeance (Romans 12:19). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds just war theory as the substantive Christian-ethical framework, rejecting both naive pacifism (which abandons the innocent to the aggressor) and unrestrained militarism (which ignores the moral constraints on warfare).

Rejects naive pacifism (abandons the innocent) and unrestrained militarism (ignores moral constraints).

etymology: The position that Christians are forbidden by Christ's teaching to use lethal force under any circumstances, including in war, self-defense, and civil punishment. biblical_def: The position that Christians are forbidden by Christ's teaching to use lethal force under any circumstances, including in war, self-defense, and civil punishment. The position appeals principally to the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:38-48, resist not evil... love your enemies), to Christ's non-resistance at His arrest (Matthew 26:52, all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword), and to the broader NT ethic of enemy-love and cross-bearing. Historically held by the Anabaptist tradition (Mennonites, Hutterites, Amish), the Quakers (Society of Friends), the Church of the Brethren, and various peace-church traditions; influential in contemporary progressive evangelicalism (Stanley Hauerwas, John Howard Yoder, the broader Anabaptist-influenced academic theology). The Reformed-confessional and broader majority-Christian response holds that Christian pacifism misreads the relevant texts: (1) the Sermon on the Mount addresses personal ethics (the individual's response to personal injury), not the magistrate's civil duty (Romans 13:4) or the soldier's lawful vocation (Luke 3:14); (2) Christ's words at His arrest concern His own redemptive submission to the cross, not a universal prohibition of lethal force; (3) the OT-NT continuity affirms the magistrate's God-given sword-bearing authority (Romans 13:1-4) and the lawfulness of the soldier's vocation (Luke 3:14; Acts 10, Cornelius the centurion is never commanded to leave his profession). The patriarchal-Reformed reader rejects Christian pacifism as misreading the personal-vs-civil distinction; the individual Christian is to love his personal enemies and not avenge personal wrongs, but the magistrate justly bears the sword and the Christian may justly serve as soldier or magistrate.

etymology: The biblical doctrine that the civil magistrate may justly execute the death penalty for certain grave crimes. Grounded in the Noahic covenant (Genesis 9:6, Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed), the Mosaic civil law, and the NT affirmation of the magistrate's sword-bearing authority (Romans 13:4).
biblical_def: The biblical doctrine that the civil magistrate may justly execute the death penalty for certain grave crimes. The foundational text is the Noahic covenant: Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man (Genesis 9:6). The grounding is significant: capital punishment for murder is grounded not in the Mosaic law (which came later) but in the universal Noahic covenant given to all mankind, and is grounded specifically in the image of God in man — the murderer who destroys an image-bearer forfeits his own life. The Mosaic civil law specified capital crimes (murder, kidnapping, certain sexual crimes, idolatry, blasphemy, etc.); the Reformed-confessional tradition (Westminster Confession XIX) distinguishes the general equity of the Mosaic judicial law (which continues to inform civil justice) from its specific Israelite-theocratic application (which has expired). The NT affirms the magistrate's continuing sword-bearing authority (Romans 13:4, he beareth not the sword in vain; the sword being the instrument of capital punishment). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine: the civil magistrate may justly execute the death penalty for murder (grounded in Genesis 9:6) and for other grave crimes as the general equity of the biblical law informs the civil order; the doctrine is grounded in the dignity of the image of God in man, not in a low view of human life; the abolitionist position that capital punishment is inherently unjust contradicts the Noahic covenant and the NT affirmation of the magistrate's sword.

The biblical-ethical doctrine holds that the unborn child is a human person bearing the image of God from the moment of conception, and that the deliberate killing of the unborn is murder, forbidden by the sixth commandment (Exodus 20:13). The biblical foundation is substantial. (1) Personhood from conception: David confesses that the LORD knit him together in his mother's womb and saw his unformed substance (Psalm 139:13-16); the LORD knew and consecrated Jeremiah before he was formed in the womb (Jeremiah 1:5); the unborn John the Baptist leaped in Elizabeth's womb at the presence of the unborn Christ (Luke 1:41-44, the unborn child responding with personal joy). (3) The Mosaic protection of the unborn: Exodus 21:22-25 provides legal protection for the unborn child harmed by violence to the mother. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine: abortion is the murder of an image-bearing human person; it is among the gravest sins of the modern age (over a billion children killed worldwide since the mid-twentieth century); the church is called to oppose it without compromise, to protect the unborn, to care for mothers in crisis, and to proclaim the gospel of forgiveness to those who have participated in abortion and repent. etymology: From Greek eu (good) + thanatos (death): the deliberate killing of a person to end suffering, whether by direct action (active euthanasia) or by deliberate withholding of ordinary care (passive euthanasia). The biblical-ethical doctrine holds that the deliberate killing of an innocent person, including for the relief of suffering, is murder forbidden by the sixth commandment.
biblical_def: From Greek eu (good) + thanatos (death): the deliberate killing of a person to end suffering. Distinguished into (1) active euthanasia (direct killing, e.g., lethal injection); (2) passive euthanasia (deliberate withholding of ordinary care with the intention of causing death); and (3) physician-assisted suicide (the physician provides the means for the patient to kill himself). The biblical-ethical doctrine holds that the deliberate killing of an innocent person, including for the relief of suffering, is murder forbidden by the sixth commandment (Exodus 20:13). The biblical foundation: (1) human life is the gift of God, not the possession of the individual to dispose of at will (Job 1:21, the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; Deuteronomy 32:39, I kill, and I make alive); (2) the deliberate killing of the innocent is murder (Exodus 20:13; Genesis 9:6); (3) suffering, while real and grievous, does not justify the taking of innocent life, and the Christian's response to suffering is the substantive ministry of presence, palliative care, and gospel hope (2 Corinthians 1:3-7; Romans 8:18). The Reformed-confessional ethic distinguishes the deliberate killing of a patient (euthanasia, forbidden) from the legitimate withholding or withdrawal of extraordinary or futile medical interventions when death is imminent and the interventions only prolong the dying process (which is not euthanasia but the acceptance of death's approach). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine: euthanasia and physician-assisted suicide are forms of murder or suicide forbidden by Scripture; the church is called to oppose them, to provide substantive care for the suffering and dying, and to proclaim the gospel hope that transforms the Christian's experience of suffering and death.

etymology: In vitro fertilization: the medical procedure by which human eggs are fertilized by sperm outside the body (in a laboratory dish) and the resulting embryos transferred to the womb. Christian bioethics engages substantive questions: the personhood of the embryo, the destruction and freezing of surplus embryos, third-party gametes, and the separation of procreation from the marital act.
biblical_def: In vitro fertilization (Latin in vitro, in glass): the medical procedure by which human eggs are fertilized by sperm outside the body in a laboratory and the resulting embryos transferred to the womb. Christian bioethics engages IVF with substantive care, recognizing both the genuine grief of infertility (a recurring biblical theme — Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, Elizabeth) and the substantive ethical questions IVF raises. The principal ethical concerns: (1) The personhood of the embryo: if human personhood begins at conception (Psalm 139:13-16), then the embryos created in IVF are human persons bearing the image of God from the moment of fertilization; this raises grave concern about the routine IVF practices of creating surplus embryos. (2) The destruction of surplus embryos: standard IVF creates more embryos than will be implanted; the surplus embryos are frozen indefinitely, discarded, or used for research — each of which, on the personhood-from-conception view, is the destruction or abandonment of a human person. (3) Embryo selection and grading: the practice of selecting the most viable embryos and discarding the rest. (4) Third-party gametes: the use of donor sperm or donor eggs introduces a third party into the procreative act, contrary to the one-flesh exclusivity of marriage. The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages IVF with discernment rather than blanket endorsement or blanket condemnation. The substantive concern is the personhood of the embryo: an IVF approach that creates only as many embryos as will be implanted, implants all of them, uses only the gametes of the married couple, and treats every embryo as a human person may be morally permissible; the standard IVF practice of creating surplus embryos for selection, freezing, and discard is gravely problematic on the personhood-from-conception view. The recurring biblical theme of the LORD's sovereign opening and closing of the womb (Genesis 30:2; 1 Samuel 1:5-6) also counsels substantive trust in the LORD's providential ordering of fruitfulness alongside the legitimate use of medical means.

etymology: The practice by which a woman bears a child for another couple or individual, whether using the surrogate's own egg (traditional surrogacy) or an embryo created from others' gametes (gestational surrogacy). Christian bioethics engages substantive concerns: the commodification of childbearing, the introduction of a third party into procreation, and the separation of motherhood into genetic, gestational, and social components.
biblical_def: The practice by which a woman bears a child for another couple or individual. Distinguished into (1) traditional surrogacy (the surrogate's own egg is used, making her the genetic and gestational mother); (2) gestational surrogacy (an embryo created from others' gametes is implanted, making the surrogate the gestational but not genetic mother). Christian bioethics engages surrogacy with substantive concern. The principal ethical concerns: (1) The commodification of childbearing: commercial surrogacy treats the womb as a rentable service and the child as a contracted product, contrary to the biblical dignity of childbearing and the child. (2) The introduction of a third party into procreation: surrogacy introduces a woman other than the wife into the procreative process, contrary to the one-flesh exclusivity of marriage. (3) The fragmentation of motherhood: surrogacy splits motherhood into genetic (egg donor), gestational (surrogate), and social (intended mother) components, contrary to the biblical integration of these in the one mother. (4) The bonding and relinquishment problem: the gestational bond between the surrogate and the child she carries is severed at birth by contract, contrary to the substantive biblical understanding of the maternal-child bond formed in the womb (Psalm 22:9-10; Isaiah 49:15). The biblical narrative of Sarah and Hagar (Genesis 16) is the cautionary OT precedent: Sarah's attempt to obtain a child through her servant Hagar produced grievous family conflict and was not the LORD's appointed means. The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages surrogacy with substantive caution: the commercial commodification of childbearing, the introduction of third parties into procreation, and the fragmentation of motherhood are substantive concerns; the genuine grief of infertility is real but does not justify the substantive ethical problems of surrogacy; adoption (the substantive biblical pattern of receiving children not biologically one's own into the covenant household) is the substantive alternative.

etymology: The biblical doctrine of the lawful grounds for divorce. The Reformed-confessional position (Westminster Confession XXIV) holds that there are two biblical grounds: adultery (Matthew 5:32; 19:9) and irremediable desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15). biblical_def: The biblical doctrine of the lawful grounds for divorce. The Reformed-confessional position (Westminster Confession XXIV.5-6) holds that marriage is a lifelong covenant designed by God to be permanent (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:6, what therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder), and that divorce is lawful only on two biblical grounds. (1) Adultery / sexual immorality: the Lord Jesus permits divorce for fornication (Greek porneia, sexual immorality; Matthew 5:32; 19:9, whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery). The innocent spouse may lawfully divorce the adulterous spouse. (2) Irremediable desertion by an unbelieving spouse: Paul permits the believing spouse to be released when the unbelieving spouse departs and will not be reconciled (1 Corinthians 7:15, But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases). The Westminster Confession (XXIV.6) summarizes: nothing but adultery, or such willful desertion as can no way be remedied by the church or civil magistrate, is cause sufficient of dissolving the bond of marriage. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed-confessional doctrine: marriage is a lifelong covenant; divorce is a grave matter permitted only on the two biblical grounds; the no-fault divorce regime of the modern West (which permits divorce for any reason or no reason) contradicts the biblical doctrine and has been catastrophic for households, children, and the broader social order. The church is called to uphold the permanence of marriage, to counsel reconciliation wherever possible, to recognize the two biblical grounds where they genuinely obtain, and to minister the gospel of grace to those wounded by divorce.

etymology: The biblical doctrine of the lawful conditions for remarriage after divorce or the death of a spouse. The Reformed-confessional position holds that the innocent party in a biblically-grounded divorce, and the widow or widower, may lawfully remarry; remarriage after an unbiblical divorce, while the former spouse lives, constitutes adultery.
biblical_def: The biblical doctrine of the lawful conditions for remarriage after divorce or the death of a spouse. The Reformed-confessional position (Westminster Confession XXIV; the broader Reformed-confessional tradition) holds: (1) Remarriage after the death of a spouse is lawful (Romans 7:2-3, if her husband be dead, she is loosed from the law of her husband... if her husband be dead, she is free from that law; so that she is no adulteress, though she be married to another man; 1 Corinthians 7:39, if her husband be dead, she is at liberty to be married to whom she will; only in the Lord). (2) Remarriage by the innocent party in a biblically-grounded divorce is lawful (the implication of Matthew 19:9, where divorce for fornication is excepted from the prohibition; the innocent party in a divorce for adultery or irremediable desertion may lawfully remarry). (3) Remarriage after an unbiblical divorce, while the former spouse lives, constitutes adultery (Matthew 5:32; 19:9; Luke 16:18, Whosoever putteth away his wife, and marrieth another, committeth adultery). The substantive question of the guilty party's remarriage is debated within the Reformed-confessional tradition: some hold the guilty party may never lawfully remarry while the innocent spouse lives; others hold the guilty party may remarry after substantive repentance. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed-confessional doctrine: remarriage is lawful for the widow/widower and for the innocent party in a biblically-grounded divorce; remarriage after an unbiblical divorce, while the former spouse lives, constitutes adultery; the church engages divorce-and-remarriage situations with substantive pastoral care, holding the biblical doctrine firmly while ministering the gospel of grace to the wounded and the repentant.

etymology: The substantive Christian-ethical debate over the moral permissibility of contraception (the deliberate prevention of conception). Positions range from the Roman Catholic prohibition of all artificial contraception, through the patriarchal-Reformed quiverfull-influenced openness-to-children position, to the broad-Protestant acceptance of contraception within marriage.
biblical_def: The substantive Christian-ethical debate over the moral permissibility of contraception (the deliberate prevention of conception within marriage). The principal positions: (1) Roman Catholic prohibition: all artificial contraception is intrinsically immoral (Humanae Vitae, 1968); only natural family planning (periodic abstinence) is permitted; the procreative and unitive purposes of the marital act may not be deliberately separated. (2) The quiverfull / openness-to-children position: influential in patriarchal-Reformed circles; children are an unqualified covenant blessing (Psalm 127:3-5), the creation mandate to be fruitful is unrescinded (Genesis 1:28), and the deliberate prevention of conception substitutes human management for divine providence over the womb. (3) The broad-Protestant acceptance: contraception within marriage is a matter of Christian liberty and prudential stewardship, distinct from abortion (the prevention of conception is morally different from the destruction of an existing person). A substantive sub-question is the distinction between contraceptive methods (which prevent conception) and abortifacient methods (which prevent the implantation of an already-conceived embryo, thereby destroying a human person); the patriarchal-Reformed reader holds firmly that abortifacient methods are gravely wrong on the personhood-from-conception view, regardless of his position on non-abortifacient contraception. The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the contraception debate with substantive seriousness: children are a covenant blessing to be received from the LORD; the creation mandate and the multigenerational-faithfulness vision counsel substantive openness to children; the deliberate, comprehensive, lifelong prevention of children within marriage (treating children as a burden to be avoided) contradicts the biblical vision; abortifacient methods are gravely wrong; but the prudential spacing of children and the substantive trust in the LORD's ordering of the womb are matters on which substantive patriarchal-Reformed Christians hold a range of positions.

etymology: The biblical doctrine of the lawful use of alcoholic beverages. Scripture presents wine and strong drink as a good gift of God to be received with thanksgiving and used in moderation (Psalm 104:15; 1 Timothy 5:23), while sternly condemning drunkenness as sin (Ephesians 5:18; Proverbs 23:29-35). Distinguished from the modern teetotal-abstinence position (total prohibition) and the libertine-excess position.
biblical_def: The biblical doctrine of the lawful use of alcoholic beverages. Scripture presents wine and strong drink in a substantively-balanced way that the patriarchal-Reformed reader holds against both the teetotal-abstinence position (total prohibition) and the libertine-excess position. The positive: wine is a good gift of God given to gladden the heart of man (Psalm 104:15, wine that maketh glad the heart of man); wine is used in the Passover and the Lord's Supper (Matthew 26:27-29); the Lord Jesus turned water into wine at Cana (John 2:1-11, His first miracle) and was accused of being a winebibber (Matthew 11:19, though falsely as to excess); Paul counsels Timothy to use a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23); wine is a sign of covenant blessing and feast-joy throughout Scripture (Deuteronomy 14:26; Amos 9:14). The negative: drunkenness is sternly condemned as sin (Ephesians 5:18, be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit; Galatians 5:21, drunkenness among the works of the flesh that exclude from the kingdom; Proverbs 23:29-35, the vivid portrait of the drunkard's misery; 1 Corinthians 6:10, drunkards shall not inherit the kingdom). The biblical doctrine: alcohol is a good gift of God to be received with thanksgiving and used in moderation; drunkenness is sin. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical balance against the modern American-evangelical teetotal-abstinence position (which arose substantially from the nineteenth-century temperance movement and lacks biblical warrant for total prohibition) and against the libertine-excess position. The substantive concern for the weaker brother (Romans 14; 1 Corinthians 8) counsels charitable consideration of those for whom alcohol is a substantive temptation, but does not establish a universal abstinence requirement.

etymology: The biblical doctrine of the proper keeping of the Sabbath / Lord's Day. The Reformed-confessional position (Westminster Confession XXI.7-8) holds that one day in seven is to be kept holy unto God; the Sabbath moved from the seventh day to the first (the Lord's Day) in commemoration of Christ's resurrection; the day is kept by rest from worldly employments and recreations and by the public and private exercises of worship.
biblical_def: The biblical doctrine of the proper keeping of the Sabbath / Lord's Day. The Reformed-confessional position (Westminster Confession XXI.7-8) holds: (1) the fourth commandment establishes a perpetual moral obligation to keep one day in seven holy unto God (Exodus 20:8-11); (2) the day moved from the seventh day (Saturday) to the first day (Sunday, the Lord's Day) in commemoration of Christ's resurrection (the apostolic pattern of first-day worship, Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10); (3) the day is kept holy by a holy resting all that day from worldly employments and recreations, and by spending the whole time in the public and private exercises of God's worship, except so much as is taken up in works of necessity and mercy (Westminster XXI.8). The Sabbath is grounded in creation (the LORD's rest on the seventh day, Genesis 2:2-3), in redemption (Israel's deliverance from Egyptian bondage, Deuteronomy 5:15), and in the new creation (Christ's resurrection on the first day). The Lord Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28) and clarifies that the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27) — correcting the Pharisaic legalistic accretions while affirming the substantive Sabbath principle. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed-confessional sabbatarian doctrine against both the antinomian position (the Sabbath is wholly abrogated; no day is holy) and the legalistic position (the Pharisaic-style multiplication of prohibitions). The substantive Sabbath observance: attendance at public worship (morning and evening where available); rest from ordinary labor and commerce; works of necessity and mercy permitted; the day given to worship, fellowship, rest, family worship, and the substantive enjoyment of the LORD.

webster_full: SABBATH OBSERVANCE, n. phr. (Christian ethics) The proper keeping of the Sabbath / Lord's Day. Reformed-confessional position (Westminster XXI.7-8): (1) the fourth commandment establishes a perpetual moral obligation to keep one day in seven holy (Exodus 20:8-11); (2) the day moved from the seventh to the first (the Lord's Day) commemorating Christ's resurrection (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10); (3) kept by holy resting from worldly employments and recreations and spending the whole time in worship, except works of necessity and mercy. Grounded in creation (Genesis 2:2-3), redemption (Deuteronomy 5:15), new creation (Christ's resurrection). Christ is Lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28); the Sabbath was made for man (Mark 2:27). Held against antinomianism and Pharisaic legalism.

corruption_summary: Sabbath observance is held against two errors: antinomianism (the Sabbath is wholly abrogated; no day is holy) and Pharisaic legalism (the multiplication of prohibitions); the biblical doctrine is the substantive keeping of the Lord's Day in rest and worship.
corruption_paragraphs: Sabbath observance is held against two opposing errors. The antinomian position (the Sabbath is wholly abrogated as Old-Covenant ceremonial law; no day is holy under the New Covenant) contradicts the Reformed-confessional doctrine that the fourth commandment establishes a perpetual moral obligation grounded in creation (Genesis 2:2-3, the LORD's rest established the Sabbath principle before the Mosaic law). The Pharisaic-legalistic position (the multiplication of detailed prohibitions, the Sabbath as a burden of rule-keeping) contradicts the Lord Jesus's correction that the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed-confessional doctrine: one day in seven kept holy unto the LORD; the day moved to the first (the Lord's Day) commemorating the resurrection; the day kept by rest from ordinary labor and commerce and by the exercises of public and private worship; works of necessity and mercy permitted; the day a substantive delight (Isaiah 58:13-14), not a burden — given to worship, fellowship, family worship, rest, and the substantive enjoyment of the LORD. The contemporary collapse of the Lord's Day into ordinary commercial-recreational activity is the substantive concern; the recovery of substantive Sabbath observance is a substantive mark of the patriarchal-Reformed household.

etymology: The biblical doctrine that solemn oaths and vows, lawfully taken, are a legitimate and sometimes-required part of Christian life, distinguished from the common profane swearing and the casual oath-taking that Christ forbids (Matthew 5:34-37). The Reformed-confessional position (Westminster Confession XXII) affirms lawful oaths and vows.
biblical_def: The biblical doctrine that solemn oaths and vows, lawfully taken, are a legitimate and sometimes-required part of Christian life. The Reformed-confessional position (Westminster Confession XXII, Of Lawful Oaths and Vows) affirms that a lawful oath is a part of religious worship, wherein the person swearing in truth, righteousness, and judgment solemnly calls God to witness what he asserts or promises (XXII.1). The biblical foundation: (1) God Himself swears by His own name (Genesis 22:16; Hebrews 6:13-17, because he could swear by no greater, he sware by himself); (2) the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles took lawful oaths (Abraham, Genesis 21:23-24; the LORD's command to swear by His name, Deuteronomy 6:13; 10:20; Paul's oaths, Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23; Galatians 1:20); (3) the third commandment regulates rather than prohibits oath-taking (Exodus 20:7, forbidding the taking of the LORD's name in vain, which presupposes the lawful taking of His name in truth). The Lord Jesus's prohibition in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:34-37, swear not at all) is understood by the Reformed-confessional tradition to forbid the casual, profane, evasive, and false oath-taking of the Pharisaic practice (swearing by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, one's head to create gradations of binding-ness and evasion), not to forbid the solemn lawful oath taken in truth before God in appropriate settings (courts of law, ordination, marriage, covenant-membership, etc.). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed-confessional doctrine: lawful oaths and vows are legitimate and sometimes required; the Christian's ordinary speech should be plain truth requiring no oath (Matthew 5:37, let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay); but the solemn lawful oath in appropriate settings is affirmed against the Anabaptist-Quaker prohibition of all oath-taking.

etymology: The biblical doctrine governing lending and the charging of interest. The OT forbade charging interest (Hebrew neshek, usury) to fellow Israelites in their poverty (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35-37; Deuteronomy 23:19-20) while permitting it to foreigners. The historic Christian and Reformed discussion distinguishes oppressive usury (forbidden) from legitimate interest on productive commercial loans (permitted by the Reformers).
biblical_def: The biblical doctrine governing lending and the charging of interest. The OT law forbade charging neshek (usury / interest) to fellow Israelites in their poverty: If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury (Exodus 22:25; cf. Leviticus 25:35-37; Deuteronomy 23:19-20, which forbids usury to a brother but permits it to a foreigner). The substantive concern of the OT law is the protection of the poor brother from exploitation in his distress; the lender is to help the poor brother freely, not to profit from his poverty. The historic Christian discussion developed substantially. The medieval Catholic church prohibited all interest-charging (treating all interest as usury), grounding the prohibition in Aristotle's argument that money is sterile and cannot lawfully breed. The Reformers (especially Calvin) made a substantive distinction: oppressive usury (charging interest to the poor in their distress, exploiting their need) remains forbidden; but legitimate interest on productive commercial loans (where the borrower uses the loan to generate profit and the lender shares in the productive return) is permissible, since the OT prohibition was specifically about the poor brother's distress, not about all interest-charging whatsoever. Calvin's substantive treatment (his letter on usury and his commentaries) distinguishes the exploitative lending the OT forbids from the legitimate commercial lending of a developed economy. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Reformed distinction: the exploitation of the poor through predatory lending (the payday-loan industry, predatory credit-card and consumer-debt practices, the broader debt-slavery of the modern financial system) is forbidden as oppressive usury; legitimate interest on productive commercial loans is permissible; the substantive biblical concern is the protection of the poor and the brother from exploitation, the warning against the bondage of debt (Proverbs 22:7, the borrower is servant to the lender), and the commendation of generous free lending to the poor brother (Deuteronomy 15:7-11; Luke 6:35).

etymology: The biblical practice of giving a tenth (tithe) of one's increase to the LORD. Established in the patriarchal period (Abraham's tithe to Melchizedek, Genesis 14:20; Jacob's vow, Genesis 28:22), codified in the Mosaic law (Leviticus 27:30-33; Numbers 18; Deuteronomy 14), and discussed in the NT. The contemporary debate concerns whether the tithe remains binding under the New Covenant or whether NT giving is governed by proportional cheerful generosity.
biblical_def: The biblical practice of giving a tenth (tithe) of one's increase to the LORD. The tithe predates the Mosaic law (Abraham's tithe to Melchizedek, Genesis 14:20, cited in Hebrews 7; Jacob's vow to tithe, Genesis 28:22), was codified in the Mosaic law (Leviticus 27:30-33, the tithe of the land belongs to the LORD; Numbers 18:21-24, the tithe given to the Levites; Deuteronomy 14:22-29, the festival tithe and the third-year poor-tithe), and is discussed in the NT (Matthew 23:23, the Lord Jesus affirms the tithe while rebuking the Pharisees for tithing herbs while neglecting justice, mercy, and faith; Hebrews 7, Abraham's tithe to Melchizedek as a type of Christ's superior priesthood). The contemporary Christian debate concerns whether the tithe remains binding under the New Covenant. (1) The continuing-tithe position: the tithe is a creation-and-patriarchal ordinance predating the Mosaic law, affirmed by Christ (Matthew 23:23), and continuing as the baseline of Christian giving; the New Covenant believer gives at least a tithe. (2) The proportional-generosity position: the specific tithe was part of the Mosaic ceremonial-civil law that has expired; NT giving is governed by proportional cheerful generosity (2 Corinthians 9:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2, as God hath prospered him), which may be more or less than a tithe depending on the believer's means. The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the debate with substantive seriousness, recognizing the substantive arguments on both sides. The substantive consensus: Christian giving should be regular, proportional, sacrificial, cheerful, and substantial; the tithe (a tenth) is a substantive and historic baseline for Christian giving; the believer of substantial means should give substantially more than a tithe; the principal substantive concern is the substantive grace of generous giving to the church, the poor, and the missionary cause (2 Corinthians 8-9), not legalistic tithe-calculation.

The continuing-tithe position holds that the tithe is a creation-and-patriarchal ordinance predating the Mosaic law (Abraham and Jacob both tithed before the law), affirmed by Christ (Matthew 23:23), and continuing as the baseline of Christian giving. The proportional-generosity position holds that the specific tithe was part of the Mosaic ceremonial-civil law (which funded the Levitical priesthood and the festival-and-poor system) that has expired with the change of the priesthood, and that NT giving is governed by proportional cheerful generosity (2 Corinthians 9:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2). The principal substantive concern is not the legalistic calculation of the tithe but the substantive grace of generous giving (2 Corinthians 8-9) to the church, the poor, and the missionary cause. The contemporary church suffers from substantive under-giving (the average professing Christian gives a fraction of a tithe); the substantive recovery is the recovery of generous, sacrificial, regular, substantial giving as a substantive grace of the Christian life.

etymology: The substantive question of how Scripture addresses slavery (Hebrew ebed, Greek doulos). The biblical material includes the regulation (not endorsement) of various ancient bond-service systems, the substantive distinction between Hebrew indentured servitude and chattel slavery, the condemnation of man-stealing, and the gospel principle that undermined ancient slavery from within (Philemon; Galatians 3:28).
biblical_def: The substantive question of how Scripture addresses slavery (Hebrew ebed, servant/slave; Greek doulos, servant/slave). The biblical material requires substantive careful reading. (1) The OT regulated rather than endorsed ancient bond-service: the Mosaic law regulated the various forms of ancient servitude (Hebrew indentured servitude to pay debts, with release in the seventh year and at Jubilee, Exodus 21:2-6; Leviticus 25:39-43; the substantive protections for servants, Exodus 21:20-21, 26-27; Deuteronomy 23:15-16, the substantive prohibition of returning an escaped slave). Hebrew servitude was substantively different from later chattel slavery: it was typically temporary (debt-bondage with release), regulated for the protection of the servant, and not based on race or kidnapping. (2) Man-stealing is condemned as a capital crime: the kidnapping and selling of persons (the basis of the transatlantic slave trade) is explicitly condemned (Exodus 21:16, he that stealeth a man, and selleth him... shall surely be put to death; 1 Timothy 1:10, menstealers among the lawless and disobedient). (3) The NT regulated the existing Roman slave system while undermining it from within: the NT addressed the universal Greco-Roman slave system (in which a substantial fraction of the population were slaves) by regulating the master-slave relationship (Ephesians 6:5-9; Colossians 3:22-4:1; 1 Peter 2:18-21) and by introducing the gospel principle that undermined the system from within (Philemon, where Paul sends the converted runaway slave Onesimus back to his master Philemon as a brother beloved; 1 Corinthians 7:21, counsel to gain freedom if possible; Galatians 3:28, the equal standing of slave and free in Christ). The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the slavery question with substantive honesty: Scripture regulated ancient bond-service systems without endorsing them as the ideal; the chattel slavery of the transatlantic trade was founded on man-stealing, which Scripture condemns as a capital crime; the gospel principle of the equal dignity of all image-bearers and the brotherhood of all believers in Christ undermined and ultimately abolished slavery wherever the gospel took deep root (the substantive role of evangelical Christians like William Wilberforce in the abolition movement); the contemporary critical use of biblical slavery material to discredit Scripture misreads the substantive distinction between regulation and endorsement and ignores Scripture's condemnation of man-stealing.

corruption_paragraphs: The substantive question of biblical slavery requires careful honest reading against two opposing distortions. The first distortion is the contemporary critical use of biblical slavery material to discredit Scripture as a pro-slavery document. This misreads the substantive distinction between regulation and endorsement: Scripture regulated the ancient bond-service systems that universally existed in the ancient world (as it regulated divorce, polygamy, and other realities) without endorsing them as the ideal; the OT Hebrew servitude system was substantively different from later chattel slavery (temporary debt-bondage with release, regulated for the servant's protection, not race-based or kidnapping-based); and crucially, Scripture condemns man-stealing — the kidnapping and selling of persons that was the foundation of the transatlantic slave trade — as a capital crime (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10). The second distortion is the historic pro-slavery misuse of Scripture by antebellum Southern theologians (including R. L. Dabney and others) to defend race-based chattel slavery; this misuse ignored the man-stealing condemnation that rendered the transatlantic trade unbiblical at its foundation and inverted the gospel principle of the equal dignity of all image-bearers. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive honest reading: Scripture regulated ancient bond-service without endorsing it; condemned the man-stealing on which chattel slavery was founded; and introduced the gospel principle (the equal dignity of all image-bearers, the brotherhood of all believers in Christ, Galatians 3:28; Philemon) that undermined and ultimately abolished slavery wherever the gospel took deep root — the substantive role of evangelical Christians like William Wilberforce, the Clapham Sect, and the broader evangelical abolition movement.

etymology: The substantive question of how the biblical material on the sojourner / stranger (Hebrew ger) bears on contemporary immigration policy. The biblical material includes commands to love and care for the sojourner (Leviticus 19:33-34), the requirement that the sojourner submit to the law of the land (Leviticus 24:22), and the affirmation of national borders and ordered nations (Acts 17:26; Deuteronomy 32:8).
biblical_def: The substantive question of how the biblical material on the sojourner / stranger (Hebrew ger) bears on contemporary immigration policy. The biblical material requires substantive balanced reading. (1) Commands to love and care for the sojourner: the Mosaic law commands Israel to love the ger (the resident foreigner who has joined Israel) as themselves, remembering that they were sojourners in Egypt (Leviticus 19:33-34; Deuteronomy 10:18-19); the sojourner is included in the gleaning provisions and the Sabbath rest (Leviticus 19:9-10; Exodus 20:10); the LORD executes justice for the sojourner (Deuteronomy 10:18). (2) The requirement that the sojourner submit to the law of the land: the ger who dwells in Israel is required to keep the same law as the native Israelite (Leviticus 24:22, ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for one of your own country; Exodus 12:48-49, the sojourner who would keep the Passover must be circumcised); the biblical ger is the assimilating sojourner who adopts the religion and law of Israel, not a foreigner maintaining a separate religious-cultural identity. (3) The affirmation of national borders and ordered nations: the LORD has determined the bounds and times of the nations (Acts 17:26; Deuteronomy 32:8); the nations are a substantive part of God's providential ordering (the table of nations in Genesis 10; the diversity of nations gathered in Revelation 7:9); national borders and ordered national life are not contrary to Scripture. The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the immigration question with substantive balance against two opposing distortions. The progressive distortion uses the love-the-sojourner texts to argue for open borders and the elimination of immigration law; this ignores the assimilation requirement (the biblical ger submits to the law and adopts the religion of the land) and the affirmation of ordered national borders. The nativist distortion ignores the substantive biblical command to love and care for the genuine sojourner. The substantive biblical position: the nation may justly maintain ordered borders and immigration law (Acts 17:26); the sojourner who comes lawfully and assimilates is to be loved and cared for (Leviticus 19:33-34); the substantive concern is ordered, lawful, assimilating immigration under just national governance, not open borders or nativist cruelty.

etymology: The biblical doctrine that the laborer is worthy of his wages and that the employer must pay the worker justly and promptly. Grounded in the Mosaic law's protection of the hired servant (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14-15), Christ's affirmation that the laborer is worthy of his hire (Luke 10:7), and James's condemnation of the defrauding of laborers (James 5:4).
biblical_def: The biblical doctrine that the laborer is worthy of his wages and that the employer must pay the worker justly and promptly. The biblical foundation: (1) The Mosaic protection of the hired servant: the wages of the hired servant must be paid promptly, not held overnight (Leviticus 19:13, the wages of him that is hired shall not abide with thee all night until the morning; Deuteronomy 24:14-15, thou shalt not oppress an hired servant that is poor and needy... At his day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it: lest he cry against thee unto the LORD, and it be sin unto thee). (2) Christ's affirmation that the laborer is worthy of his hire (Luke 10:7; 1 Timothy 5:18, applied to the support of ministers). (3) James's condemnation of wage-fraud (James 5:4, Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth). The biblical doctrine of the just wage: the worker is worthy of his wages; the employer must pay justly and promptly; the defrauding or oppression of workers is a grave sin that cries out to the LORD. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine against two opposing distortions. The exploitative-employer distortion oppresses the worker through wage-theft, the withholding of wages, and the systematic underpayment of the vulnerable. The socialist distortion treats the just-wage principle as warrant for the abolition of private property, the state-mandated equalization of outcomes, or the labor-theory-of-value economics of Marx. The substantive biblical position: the worker is worthy of his wages; the employer has a substantive moral duty to pay justly and promptly; this duty operates within (not against) the biblical affirmation of private property (Exodus 20:15, 17), lawful commerce, and the freedom of contract; the just wage is the substantive obligation of the godly employer, not the warrant for socialist economics.

etymology: The biblical doctrine requiring honesty and integrity in commerce, particularly in the use of accurate weights and measures. Grounded in the repeated Mosaic command for just balances (Leviticus 19:35-36; Deuteronomy 25:13-16) and the wisdom-literature condemnation of false weights (Proverbs 11:1; 20:10, 23). A substantive symbol of commercial integrity and honest dealing.
biblical_def: The biblical doctrine requiring honesty and integrity in commerce, particularly in the use of accurate weights and measures. In the ancient world, merchants weighed goods and money on balances; a dishonest merchant could use a heavy weight when buying (to receive more) and a light weight when selling (to give less), or use deceptive measures — defrauding the customer through false standards. The biblical command is emphatic and repeated. (1) The Mosaic law commands just weights and measures: Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in meteyard, in weight, or in measure. Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have (Leviticus 19:35-36); Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small... But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have... For all that do such things, and all that do unrighteously, are an abomination unto the LORD thy God (Deuteronomy 25:13-16). (2) The wisdom literature condemns false weights: A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight (Proverbs 11:1; cf. 16:11; 20:10, 23). (3) The prophets condemn commercial fraud: Amos condemns those who make the ephah small and the shekel great and falsify the balances by deceit (Amos 8:5); Micah condemns the wicked balances and the bag of deceitful weights (Micah 6:11). The just-weights doctrine is a substantive symbol of the broader principle of commercial integrity and honest dealing in all of life. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine: honesty and integrity in commerce is a substantive moral obligation; the false balance is an abomination to the LORD; the just weight is His delight; commercial fraud (in all its modern forms — deceptive advertising, fraudulent accounting, misrepresentation of goods, hidden fees, dishonest contracts) is a grave sin; the godly man deals honestly in all his commerce, and the just weight is a substantive mark of his integrity before the LORD.

etymology: The biblical principle that the one who has wronged another by theft, fraud, or damage must make restitution — restoring what was taken plus an additional penalty. Grounded in the Mosaic restitution laws (Exodus 22:1-15; Leviticus 6:1-7; Numbers 5:5-7) and exemplified in Zacchaeus's fourfold restitution (Luke 19:8).
biblical_def: The biblical principle that the one who has wronged another by theft, fraud, or damage must make restitution — restoring what was taken plus an additional penalty. The Mosaic restitution laws are detailed and substantive. (1) Theft requires multiplied restitution: the thief must restore double for a stolen item still in his possession, fourfold for a stolen sheep, fivefold for a stolen ox (Exodus 22:1-4); the principle is that the thief restores more than he took, bearing the cost of his crime. (2) Fraud and false dealing require restitution plus a fifth: If a soul sin... and lie unto his neighbour in that which was delivered him to keep, or in fellowship, or in a thing taken away by violence, or hath deceived his neighbour... he shall restore that which he took violently away... or all that about which he hath sworn falsely; he shall even restore it in the principal, and shall add the fifth part more thereto (Leviticus 6:1-5; Numbers 5:5-7). (3) Damage to another's property requires restitution (Exodus 22:5-6, 14). The NT exemplifies restitution in Zacchaeus the tax collector, who, upon his conversion, declared: if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold (Luke 19:8) — demonstrating that genuine repentance produces substantive restitution. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive biblical doctrine: genuine repentance for theft, fraud, or damage produces substantive restitution; the wrongdoer restores what was taken (plus the biblical penalty where applicable); restitution is the substantive fruit of repentance, distinct from the gratuitous forgiveness of the gospel (the gospel forgives the guilt of sin freely through Christ; restitution addresses the substantive temporal-civil obligation to the wronged party). The contemporary therapeutic-evangelical neglect of restitution (treating repentance as a merely-internal emotional experience with no substantive obligation to make material amends) contradicts the substantive biblical doctrine; genuine repentance produces Zacchaeus-style restitution.

corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary therapeutic-evangelical neglect of restitution treats repentance as a merely-internal emotional experience (feeling sorry for sin) with no substantive obligation to make material amends to the wronged party. This contradicts the substantive biblical doctrine. The Mosaic restitution laws are detailed and substantive: the thief restores multiplied (double, fourfold, fivefold; Exodus 22:1-4); the defrauder restores the principal plus a fifth (Leviticus 6:5; Numbers 5:7); damage to property is made good (Exodus 22:5-6). The NT exemplifies the principle in Zacchaeus, whose genuine repentance immediately produced substantive restitution: if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold (Luke 19:8). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine while carefully distinguishing two things. The gospel forgives the guilt of sin freely and completely through the substitutionary work of Christ; the believer's eternal standing before God rests on Christ's righteousness alone, not on his restitution. But genuine repentance produces substantive restitution to the wronged party as its fruit; the believer who has stolen, defrauded, or damaged another has a substantive temporal-civil obligation to make material amends. The thief who is converted returns the stolen goods; the defrauder who repents makes the defrauded party whole; the one who has damaged another's property restores the damage. Restitution is the substantive fruit of repentance, the substantive demonstration that the repentance is genuine and not merely emotional. The patriarchal-Reformed household and church teaches and practices substantive restitution as a substantive mark of genuine repentance.
